newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Security tight as Dublin stages song contest.
newsitem.headline: Security tight as Dublin stages song contest.

text.p: Fears of a guerrilla attack on the Eurovision Song Contest prompted strict security arrangements in Dublin on Saturday with hundreds of police posted at the theatre where the annual music competition is being staged.

Police and security experts have been guarding the Point Theatre twenty-four hours a day ahead of the event and around 400 police were expected to be on duty when the contest is broadcast live to an estimated 300 million viewers around the world on Saturday evening.
Irish President Mary Robinson and Prime Minister John Bruton will be among 3,000 spectators at the theatre in Dublin.
Entrants from 25 countries, most of them European, are taking part in the competition this year, fighting for the honour of winning the prize for the best song.

The Irish Times said the event's organisers fear that Protestant guerrillas, who oppose any move to unite British-ruled Northern Ireland with the Irish Republic, may attempt to disrupt the Eurovision competition with a bomb scare in retaliation for recent IRA action in Britain.

The Irish Republican Army, fighting to end British rule of Northern Ireland, forced the postponement of the famous Grand National horse steeplechase in April with a hoax bomb warning and has disrupted Britain's travel network several times in recent weeks with a series of bomb attacks and hoax calls.

Traffic will be tightly controlled during the contest and spectators will be searched, the Irish Times said. It said police hoped the stringent security arrangements would allow them to dismiss any bomb warning as a hoax.
"There is a lot of security at the building, just to make sure," a spokesman for the competition told Reuters.

Ireland has won the contest four times in the last five years. The winning country stages the event the following year, and Ireland's success has led to some grumbles in the country about the cost of repeatedly holding the competition.
But ominously for the finances of Ireland's national broadcasting network, which shoulders most of the cost, Dublin bookmakers see Ireland as joint favourite to win the title once again.
